scopeReview: CED FUN-2.A.1–2: differentiability implies continuity; a continuous function can lack a finite derivative. Covers corners, vertical tangent, excluded base point, point mismatch and direct quotient tests. No later derivative rules required.
varietyReview: Tests implication/counterexamples, a corner, cube-root vertical tangent, a jump, missing-domain cancellation, differentiable absolute-value product, an original corner graph, reconstructing a function limit, two join parameters, a limit of nearby derivatives trap and damped oscillation.
repetitionReview: Each prompt and all four options were read separately; distinct tasks/contexts within this set. Cross-topic exact duplicates checked by validator. Semantic similarity and AP difficulty remain judgment calls, not proven by an automated score.

questions.independentReasoning: Check the implication by multiplying the defining quotient back by h, rather than merely restating the theorem. Counterexamples |x−a|, f(x)=x+7 and f(x)=x verify the failure of the three stronger or reversed claims.
optionReview: A finite derivative forces the output increment to approach zero with the input increment.
A continuous corner such as |x−a| can lack a derivative.
A derivative controls local change, not the function’s height.
A continuous nonhorizontal line has a nonzero derivative.

check.expectedAnswer: If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.

questions.independentReasoning: Use the actual point value f(2)=0 and substitute x=2+h before dividing. Sign analysis of h gives two different exact constants. Continuity follows from |h|→0, independently of the failed derivative limit.
optionReview: A zero height does not determine a slope, and the two quotient limits disagree.
The quotient |h|/h has limits −1 and 1 from the two increment directions.
The ordinary derivative requires the left-hand quotient to agree.
The ordinary derivative also requires the right-hand quotient.

questions.independentReasoning: Check the real cube-root identity on both signs of h; squaring the cube root makes the denominator positive. The original function tends to its finite value zero, but its normalized increment is unbounded. An infinite slope notation is not a finite ordinary derivative.
optionReview: The real cube root is defined for negative inputs as well.
The actual value is ∛0=0.
Both sides have an unbounded positive quotient, so no finite derivative value exists.
The necessity goes the other way: differentiability implies continuity.

check.expectedAnswer: Its difference quotient 1/(∛h)² grows without bound, giving a vertical tangent rather than a finite slope.

questions.independentReasoning: Compute the two branch limits and assigned value separately. A jump remains regardless of the smoothness of each branch away from the join. The theorem’s contrapositive, discontinuity implies nondifferentiability, is used correctly; no converse is assumed.
optionReview: Polynomial branches can join differentiably when the boundary conditions match.
A positive height does not obstruct a derivative.

check.expectedAnswer: It is discontinuous there: the left-hand limit is 1 while f(1) and the right-hand limit are 3.

questions.independentReasoning: Distinguish equality on a punctured domain from equality of functions including the base input. The original f(1) is absent. A separately filled line has a well-defined derivative, showing precisely which extra operation the student silently performed.
optionReview: Cancellation gives nearby values but does not add the missing point to the domain.
Cancellation is valid for the nearby inputs x≠1.
A height is not a derivative, and the original missing value still prevents the definition.
The difference quotient requires the actual base value f(1).

check.expectedAnswer: The original function has no value at 1, so its derivative at 1 is undefined; the filled extension is a different function at that input.

questions.independentReasoning: Cancel only the nonzero increment h, leaving its absolute value, not a sign ratio. The remaining quantity is nonnegative and tends to zero from both directions. This direct limit also implies continuity and disproves the proposed blanket rule about absolute values.
optionReview: The quotient is |h|, not the sign quotient |h|/h.
Its difference quotient at 0 equals |h|, which tends to zero from both sides.
Negative inputs do not produce a negative limiting quotient in this example.
Multiplying by x changes the local quotient and removes the corner obstruction here.

questions.independentReasoning: Compute heights and slopes as separate tests from the actual graph vertices. The included vertex is shared, but the local rises/runs give unequal slopes. The original graph is hash-bound; its corner, rather than an invented missing point, supports the conclusion.
optionReview: Finite differentiability cannot occur without continuity.
A filled matching point does not ensure equal branch slopes.
The matching heights give continuity while unequal quotient limits prevent a derivative.
Unequal slopes do not by themselves destroy continuity of the joined graph.

check.expectedAnswer: Continuous but not differentiable: both branches meet at height 1, but their slopes are 2 and −1.

questions.independentReasoning: Multiply the quotient by h and use h→0 to recover the output increment. The product tends to zero despite a nonzero derivative. Adding back the known base value gives 9, ruling out the slope, zero and insufficient-information alternatives.
optionReview: This confuses the limiting rate with the function height.

The existing finite derivative implies continuity, so the limit equals the assigned value.

Substitution of (a,b)=(0,1) gives a constant left branch and a quadratic right branch with a common zero slope. Each other pair fails a height or slope test explicitly, proving uniqueness.
